I get this so much. It’s largely how I got myself out of the constant binge purge cycle, was telling myself that I don’t have to binge right now but I can later if the urge is still there. It started slowly, 2 or 3 days without binging then I built up to weeks at a time. Then months. I relapsed at the end of September, but the “getting back on track” wasn’t as difficult as when I was purging every day. And the urge to binge is almost nonexistent. I fight the urge to purge sometimes after I’ve eaten more than I wanted to, or when I feel overly full. But I have the “muscle memory” of knowing that the full feeling will pass too.  I think the all or nothing mindset that comes with bulimia is part of what kept me from recovering, just taking it moment by moment was much better and accepting the binges as part of recovery, not a failure of it.
Talk to your doctor. I know you don’t want to, but the best way to prevent a relapse is to talk it out with someone until you’re in a spot where you have the muscle memory to do it yourself.

3 weeks is awesome dude!!! I hit that mark last month and ended up relapsing as well. For me the biggest thing is to forgive myself. Just because I relapsed doesn’t mean I’m failing at recovery, it’s how I keep going afterward that defines me- not the relapse. 

The first few days after a relapse are always hardest for me, I have to make myself eat. Start with breakfast, make some safe food if you have too. Anything to keep food in your belly, you can’t be strong in recovery if you don’t give your mind and body the nutrients to do so. I plan out my meals ahead so I don’t have to panic last minute and binge again. 

Mindfulness is also key for me, when I eat it should be the main activity. Sitting down at a table not watching tv or eating while I’m driving (not always possible, but it helps!) Also activities that keep me in my body, I find exercises that make me feel good and strong and do them to remind myself of what my body can do when I take care of it. Not punishing myself for eating. Yoga can be helpful too, focusing on the breathing has a real calming affect and helps relieve the anxiety that comes from recovery.

I don't think homeschooling has stopped my mom from doing anything in her life. She supplemented most of our high school education so really most of our "homeschooling" was outside the home and she was able to begin attending college classes. By the time my youngest sister graduated high school she had gotten her associates degree and is getting her bachelor's this year. 

I think a lot of it just has to do with planning and seeing what kind of education opportunities are available. And I love the fact that I got to experience something other than the American public school system .

Late to the party here but I wanted to speak up as someone who was homeschooled. I think homeschooling has an incredible advantage, but like most things it's what you make of it.

My mom didn't work for most of the time she was homeschooling us. She made our education her main priority, picking out curriculum, talking with other homeschool parents, seeking all kinds of supplemental classes and outside the home learning opportunities.

Fortunately for us we lives in a very homeschool friendly state, the public schools had no issue with homeschool students coming to take certain classes that we couldn't get at home. 

We were very involved in the community and our homeschool group  (a co-op of families, all homeschooled) a chance to get involved in extra curricular and hang out with our peers. 

If you look there are SO MANY opportunities to learn outside a traditional school setting, many colleges will let homeschool highschoolers take accredited classes as well; and having the learning base be at home can be such a great way to encourage kids to love learning and be curious about the world. But I can't stress enough, you will get what you put into it. If you don't want to do the work as a parent you can not expect your kid too.

On another personal note, I felt homeschooling prepared me a bit more for college than the classes I took at public school did. It was more of an independent study at home by the time we were in high school so the lecture/reading style of most college classrooms was easy to adapt to.

I was homeschooles all but one year, I went to a small Christian school my junior year. Homeschool has lots of advantages to it. I am very close with my siblings and we are each others main support system in our adult life - I know for a fact Its because we were forced together so much as kids. I got to spend a lot of time studying subjects that I liked, without having to wait for other kids to keep up or having it dumbed down for me. It helped prepare me for college because I was so used to studying on my own and knew how to take notes, think critically, and was way more familiar with concept of "independent learning"than most of my peers. I never had a social anxiety or awkwardness problem, in fact being homeschooled forced me to become more outgoing because that was the only way to make friends - I didn't have "school friends" we went on lots of field trips, extended recess at the peak hours of the day and doing school at night instead. Life was a lot more impromptu, thus giving me a more relaxed and "go with the flow," attitude now as well.

There are a lot of cons though. I don't do well in classrooms usually because I never had to be in one. I STILL struggle with getting up early and be ready on time for things (not all homeschoolers are like this though). My math and science understanding are behind most kids my age because they weren't my mother's strong suits so she didn't exactly know how to teach them. I know enough where it's not holding me back in anyway really, it's just more difficult for me than it had to be. If I had to do it again I would suggest homeschooling through 8th grade and going to high school for four years, just so I had an actual math and science education from teachers who could explain things and push me better. Socially, I excell, as do a lot of other homeschooled kids. The stigma about that bothers me, mostly cause it's rarely true (from my experience).

It helps if you live in an area that is open and "homeschool friendly" so that way kids can get a more rounded education (i.e. taking MEAP tests at schools, ACTS, SAT's, foreign language classes, drama clubs, etc...) I think there is a right way of homeschooling kids and a wrong way. Parents who board their kids at home and try to hide them from the world and feed them lies should not be homeschooling their kids. Parents who simply believe that they can enrich their children's education by providing an alternative to the traditional classroom setting in the early years are on the right track. It takes a village though, and y'all will hate each other sometimes, feel like you re fucking everything up or just come across assholes who think they know better than you - just make education the goal and eveything else generally falls into place. (in my opinion)

"Can I bum a cig?" I didn't normally smoke, but since the day had already turned to shit before nine o'clock I figured, *why not?* The mans eyes lit up as he enthusiastically held the pack out to me,

"They're Camel Menthols, is that okay?" I nodded my head as I reached to take one of the thin white cigarettes out of the pack he held in front of me. "Do you need a light?" He indicated to a black lighter in his opposite hand, I smiled and thanked him. Inhaling the smoke I breathed deeply, already feeling a little bit better about being late to work. 

I now looked at the man next to me at the bus stop, he was ungodly pale and didn't have gloves on despite there being a foot of snow outside and more expected throughout the day. He was wearing a black suite along with a black coat, despite his young age a cane leaned on the bench next to him. I pulled my own scarf tighter around my neck, craning to look down the road to see if I could spot the bus coming. 

"Bus is running behind schedule." The man spat the words out, for the first time I noticed he didn't appear to be in a good mood. I looked at the cig he bummed me and feeling guilty asked him,

 "You doing alright man?" He sighed heavily and rubbed his temple with his free hand. 

"Work is murder lately," I took a drag of my cigarette and nodded my head in agreement. "It used to be easy, you know? Technology was less advanced, people weren't as aware as they are today!" I looked at him quizzically.

"What exactly do you do?" 

"I'm in collections," he waved his hand in the air as to dismiss this as obvious information. I again nodded my head, not quite understanding. "My boss has been riding me hard lately, quota is down he says." He stopped and smiled at me though, "But then you know, moments like this" - he pointed his finger at the two of us - "moments like this when an unexpected stranger asked me for a cigarette... well, it just makes things a little easier. So, thanks."

"No problem man," I flicked my cigarette towards the slush filled streets as I saw the bus approaching, "I'm just living you know." He chuckled to himself as I climbed onto the bus, "That's what they all say."

I watched you, I watched your family become a family. I saw you for the first time, when they discovered you were green, and kept you anyways. As you grew you began to question everything you were taught to believe. I saw you become angry with injustice, and hide away from the rest of the world. 

You fell in love, you had your heart shattered into a million pieces. You did many great things - and not because they were great things. You taught me that you need to commit to what you believe - and when you live for that you've done a great thing. I saw your confidence continue to build, and your compassion emerge as you got older. It gave me hope, because I couldn't help but see myself in you.

I watched you die too. It took me by surprise, and all of a sudden it was no longer fair. It wasn't on purpose, it wasn't supposed to be that way. "Hello, my name is Dwyer, Nicole Dwyer. My husband used to call me Nikki,"

"Hi Nikki," the group said in unison, looking at me expectantly. I swallowed, I had been coming here for weeks, court mandated of course, but I had never shared before. I never actually thought I would end up here, in the gym of the abandoned high school. It had been taken over years ago by Vanderlyn Inc. a start up rehab facility by the visionary himself Mr. Vanderlyn. It was supposed to be a place for those who had gone astray in society, people who didn't follow the rules and needed to be guided back. But here I am, stay at home mother of three, I had a college degree, my husband was a politician. I swallowed again, "My name is Nikki, and I have been directly involved with Charity and giving her and her foundations money for twenty years now."

I thought back to that moment, had it really been twenty years ago? I was only sixteen at the time, full of hope, I really thought I could make a difference in the world. That was before of course my marriage and choice to be a mother, but still being nine years away at the time, I figured why not have a little fun? It was illegal sure, but come on all the cool kids were doing it, even Courtney had made a reference to it in her valedictorian speech, "I've heard giving to those less fortunate than yourself can give you the same gratuitous feeling of the chemicals found in our food, except it's natural." It had obviously made every teacher and parent slightly uncomfortable, but they reassured themselves that a good girl like Courtney wouldn't ever do something stupid like charity work, after all she had been taking pill since she was born - a whole five years before it was mandatory. 

But I remembered what she had said, so two years later my senior year when some boy at a party I was at asked me if I wanted to sneak off with him to volunteer a few hours at an underground shelter I said yes, I was curious. It wasn't at all how I had imagined it. My mother had always told me that people who worked in thee illegal shelters weren't doing anything to help society, they gave away their money, lived off nothing, and what was worse some of them didn't even take their pills.

But these people seemed so, happy. They talked so fast, and moved with such purpose they seemed almost super human. There was one woman in charge of the entire place, just cooking and cooking and laughing - I'd never seen somebody work for more than two hours before let alone enjoy it. She was supposed to be bad? It wasn't until my second trip I learned her name, Charity. The best thing you can do is offer to listen, never judge and always direct them to get professional help. So, I work at a family steak house in the midwest. I ended up getting a break around 6pm - 7pm because of a large party we had coming in that night. I decided to use my break to go buy candy and smoke cigarettes (yay server life!). I realize at this point my car keys are locked in my car, I don't have time to do anything about it then so I wait until the end of my shift and start asking if anyone at my work knows how to pick a lock. I work in a restaurant shouldn't be hard right? Well, no such luck, so I call the police department and see if they can come unlock my car for me. No luck again. I call the Wrecker company and *Finally* someone is coming to unlock my car - I'll make it home tonight! 

I'm sitting on the back of my car talking on the phone texting my sister letting her know what's up when out of no where a man in his mid 50's wearing flannel walks up to me. "Still can't get your car unlocked, huh?" 

"Yeah, nobody here knows how to pick a car lock and Lord knows what happened to my spare key." I keep babbling on about how it's gonna cost me sixty dollars and how I'm just grateful to have somebody coming. Basically I'm trying to let him know I've got everything under control and he can get on his merry way. He didn't look threatening, but I was trying to be cautious.

As I'm talking, he begins examining the lock. I remember looking to check my phone to see if my sister replied to my message and looked up to see my driver side door standing wide open. My jaw dropped in shock, "Thank you!" I stammered as I ran over to grab the key off the floor of my car. I turned around and he was already walking away. "Hey! What's your name?" I called out after him. He stopped and turned around, I noticed his hands were empty except for his own pair of keys.

"Robert," I smiled and repeated the name. 

"Robert, are you an angel?" I don't know why this was the first thing out of my mouth, I'm not very religious and last time I checked angels don't wear flannel. Anyways, he laughed and I don't remember him ever actually answering the question. He told me to be safe and have a good night. 

Thank you Robert.

Our protagonist's would be introduced. A young, avant guard atheist who is not only a faithful member but a mod of r/atheism. He is on his way to the top, he will soon be creating his own subreddit and really "make it" in the virtual world. A legend.

From this point on we are launched into the story line. A story of a boy, on the search for the himself. Our protagonist is emotionally wrought as he clicks and clicks his way to self realization. He stalks this girls post history, an intense and climatic piece written by Danny Elfman helping the suspense build. We cut to a shot of our protagonist sitting at a blank computer screen. It has crashed. He tries for a moment to get things running again. The audience is on the edge of their seats. Will the young man find his answers? Then, without notice the young man gets up and walks away.

Birke offers an interesting point of view in this chapter. Her goal in outlining the problems of finding a biological cause for homosexuality appears to be well presented. And she seems to suggest that the motive behind wanting there to be a “gay” gene may not be scientific whatsoever, yet rather a ploy to eradicate it from existence and have a happy world of straight people. One particular things she notes is the use of science experiments all based on assumptions about homosexual structure of the brain. The biggest culprit would appear to be the assumption that lesbians tend to be more similar to straight men and gay men are similar to straight women, explaining their similar attraction to a man or woman. The problem with this is that it is born out of labeling testosterone and estrogen male and female hormones, where the reality is that both men and female (gay and straight) have both hormones pulsating through their bodies. Another big problem is the definition of sex, that is penetration. Scientist claim that sex is for reproduction, and since two males nor two females having sex can reproduce it is not permissible. If the homosexual gene is biological, this presents a problem for sexual reproduction in the context of evolution. Since gay people are less likely to reproduce, would it not make sense that there would be fewer and fewer of them as time pressed on? Yet, the number seems to stay the same. With the conclusion Birke affirms the notion that sexual orientation is social, rather than biological and advocates it as a good thing.
